name: Table Topics
description: The classic Toastmasters impromptu-speaking segment: respond to a surprise question or topic with a 1-2 minute structured mini-speech. Trains thinking on your feet, structure under pressure, and composure.
instructions: 1) One person (the Topicsmaster) prepares a list of questions/topics unknown to speakers. 2) A speaker is called up and given the topic only when they reach the front. 3) Speak for 1-2 minutes: open with a clear position, give 1-2 supporting points or a short story, and end with a conclusion that ties back to the topic. 4) A timer signals green at 1:00, yellow at 1:30, red at 2:00. 5) Rotate through speakers; optionally have an evaluator give 1 minute of feedback each. Solo version: use a random question generator and a phone timer, record yourself.
setup: topic list or random question generator; timer
variations: Themed topics; follow-on responses; story-completion prompts; object prompts

name: Table Topics: Story Starter
description: A Table Topics variant where the Topicsmaster starts a story and each speaker improvises the next chapter. Trains narrative impromptu speaking and listening.
instructions: 1) The leader opens a story with a line like 'It was a dark and stormy night...' 2) Call a speaker to the front to continue the story for 1-2 minutes, advancing the plot. 3) Call the next speaker to pick up exactly where the last left off. 4) The final speaker must bring the story to an ending. 5) Debrief on which transitions and details worked.
variations: Give each speaker 4 required random words; audience guesses the required words afterward

name: Table Topics: Mystery Object Bag
description: Speakers draw an unseen object from a bag and must speak about it immediately. Trains description, invention, and confidence with zero prep.
instructions: 1) Fill a bag with varied objects (vintage items work well: rotary phone dial, slide, coin, kitchen gadget). 2) Speaker draws an object without looking (or is blindfolded and must identify it by feel). 3) Speak 1-2 minutes: what it is, how it's used, a story or argument built around it. 4) For coins: speak about the mint year - something from history or your life that year.
variations: Blindfolded feel-and-describe; coins with mint years; Guinness world-record prompts ('describe the record you broke')

name: One Minute Off-the-Cuff
description: Record yourself giving a totally unprepared one-minute speech on a random topic. The core solo drill for off-the-cuff comfort.
instructions: 1) Generate a random topic (random word generator, or have a friend text you one). 2) Set a 60-second timer and hit record on your phone. 3) Speak continuously: take a position, support it, conclude. No stopping except to breathe; if you run out, make something up but stay on topic. 4) Listen back; note fillers, dead ends, and whether you landed an ending. 5) Repeat daily with new topics. Beginners start at 30 seconds; advanced go to 2-3 minutes.
origin: common speaker-training drill; popularized in speaking blogs and The Laughing Classroom (Loomans & Kolberg)
variations: Add the no-filler challenge: restart the timer every time you say um/uh/like

name: 30 Seconds Filler-Free
description: Speak for 30 seconds with zero filler words; restart on every slip. Builds the pause habit that replaces um/uh/like.
instructions: 1) Pick any topic and hit record. 2) Speak for 30 seconds with no filler words (um, uh, like, you know, so). 3) The moment you use one, stop and start over from zero. 4) Do this until you complete 10 clean runs. 5) Graduate to 60 seconds, then 2 minutes. Key technique: when you feel a filler coming, pause silently instead.
origin: speaker-coaching drill (The Speaker Lab and others)
variations: Pair version: partner dings a bell at each filler; Toastmasters 'Ah-Counter' role does this for a whole meeting

name: Triple Speak
description: Speak on a random word, then smoothly transition to a second and third random word mid-speech. Trains coherent continuous speech and graceful topic transitions.
instructions: 1) Group brainstorms a board of random nouns everyone knows (e.g., moon, catfish, Kanye West). 2) Speaker stands with back to the board and is given one word to start speaking about - anything coherent and continuous. 3) After ~15 seconds (or when they slow), the leader calls a second word; the speaker must transition smoothly to it. 4) After 15 more seconds, a third word is given; the speaker transitions and must conclude the speech on it. 5) No speech is 'wrong'. Optionally vote for a favorite, and the winner retells theirs with 2 new audience-chosen words inserted.
origin: Chicago Debates / National Association for Urban Debate Leagues coaching resource
variations: Solo: use a random word generator that you glance at every 20 seconds

name: Philosophical Chairs
description: A whole-room standing debate where participants physically move between Agree/Disagree corners as arguments persuade them. Trains persuasive argument and listening.
instructions: 1) Brainstorm a list of debatable resolutions (e.g., 'Football should be banned'). 2) Read one; everyone walks to a corner: Strongly Agree, Agree, Disagree, Strongly Disagree; undecided stay in the middle. 3) Alternate short speeches from each side, starting with the strong corners. 4) Anyone moved by an argument physically changes corners; speakers aim to pull the undecideds. 5) The round ends when no undecideds remain in the middle.
origin: classroom debate pedagogy; Chicago Debates / NAUDL
variations: Two-corner version; rule that you must restate the previous speaker's point before adding yours

name: SPAR Debate
description: A compressed two-person debate format on a just-announced resolution with minutes of prep. The standard entry drill for argument construction and rebuttal.
instructions: 1) Pair up; assign a simple resolution (serious or silly: 'Cats are better than dogs', 'Homework should be abolished') and sides. 2) Give 2-4 minutes prep. 3) Format: Affirmative opening (1-2 min), Negative opening (1-2 min), optional cross-examination (1 min each), rebuttals (1 min each), closing statements (30-60 sec each). 4) Audience or judge votes and names the single most persuasive moment. 5) Swap sides or partners and repeat with a new resolution.
origin: competitive debate training; widely used by urban debate leagues and classrooms (Facing History, Argument-Centered Education)
variations: Silly-topic SPAR for beginners; 30-second 'micro-SPAR' rounds; switch-sides rematch on the same topic

name: Shadow Debate
description: Pause a recorded debate after each argument and deliver your own rebuttal aloud before hearing the real one. Solo rebuttal training with a built-in answer key.
instructions: 1) Find a recorded debate (e.g., WSDC finals or any championship round on YouTube). 2) Play one speech; pause after each distinct argument. 3) Stand up and verbally refute the argument as if you were the opposing speaker. 4) Resume the video and compare your rebuttal to the actual response - note structures or responses better than yours. 5) Repeat through the whole round; redo weekly with new rounds.
origin: competitive debate coaching (Vancouver Debate Academy and others)
variations: Do it with TV interviews or panel shows; rebut op-ed articles paragraph by paragraph aloud

name: Shrinking Speech (Rebuttal Redo)
description: Give the same speech repeatedly with less and less time, forcing ruthless efficiency in word choice and argument selection.
instructions: 1) Prepare and deliver a 5-minute speech (or rebuttal). 2) Immediately redo the same content in 4 minutes. 3) When you can do it cleanly in 4, cut to 3, then 2:30. 4) Finally deliver it once more at the original 5 minutes - notice how much calmer, clearer, and better-prioritized it is. The drill forces you to identify what actually matters and to communicate efficiently.
variations: Reverse version: expand a 1-minute speech to 3 minutes by adding evidence and examples, not padding

name: Flash Drills (30-Second Prep Speeches)
description: Draw a debate motion, take 30 seconds to think, then deliver a one-minute opening speech. Trains rapid case construction.
instructions: 1) Write 10-20 debate motions on slips of paper (or use an online motion bank). 2) Draw one; start a 30-second prep timer - decide your position and 2 arguments. 3) Deliver a 1-minute opening speech: state the motion, your stance, and your arguments with brief support. 4) Draw the next motion immediately. Do 5-10 in a row. 5) Record and review one per session.
setup: motion slips or online motion list, timer
variations: Escalate by cutting prep to 10 seconds; or require exactly 3 arguments every time

name: Get the Gist (Summarization Drill)
description: Listen to a long talk and restate its main points aloud in under a minute. Trains listening, synthesis, and the summarizing skill used in Q&A and rebuttal.
instructions: 1) Play a 10-20 minute talk or lecture (TED talks work well). 2) Take minimal notes - key claims only. 3) When it ends, stand and deliver a 30-60 second spoken summary of its core argument and support, as if briefing someone who missed it. 4) Re-watch skimming to check what you missed or distorted. 5) Harder version: summarize after only one listen with no notes.
variations: Summarize for different audiences: a child, an expert, a skeptic

name: Dr. Know-It-All
description: Three people answer audience questions as one 'world's smartest person', speaking one word each in turn. Trains listening, acceptance, and quick verbal construction.
instructions: 1) Three speakers stand shoulder to shoulder as 'Dr. Know-It-All'. 2) The audience asks questions ('Why is the sky blue?'). 3) The trio answers one word at a time, left to right, building grammatical sentences collaboratively. 4) Answers end when a player says a clear final word; the group bows. 5) Rotate trios every few questions.
origin: improv theatre game adopted by debate/speech coaches
variations: Expert press-conference variant: one person answers as an absurd expert, others play journalists

name: PowerPoint Karaoke
description: Present a slide deck you have never seen, improvising authoritative narration for each surprise slide. Trains composure, transitions, and confident delivery regardless of content.
instructions: 1) Someone prepares (or downloads) decks of 5-10 random, unrelated slides; presenters must not preview them. 2) Presenter takes the clicker and delivers a confident presentation, inventing a through-line as each slide appears. 3) Rules: no breaking character, treat every slide as if you planned it, land a conclusion on the final slide. 4) 3-5 minutes per presenter; audience applauds the most committed performance. 5) Debrief: where did confidence carry weak content?
setup: projector and pre-made random slide decks
origin: tech/comedy community game (Zentrale Intelligenz Agentur, Berlin 2006); now a standard presentation-training exercise
variations: Solo: auto-advance a stranger's slideshare deck and record yourself; themed decks for work teams

name: Fable Retelling (Progymnasmata I)
description: First exercise of the ancient rhetoric curriculum: retell a short fable in your own words, expanded and compressed, with its moral. Trains command of narrative material and flexible expression.
instructions: 1) Pick a short Aesop fable. 2) Retell it aloud in your own words faithfully. 3) Retell it again EXPANDED: add dialogue, description, and invented speeches for the characters. 4) Retell it COMPRESSED: 30 seconds, bare essentials. 5) State the moral in one crisp sentence, then defend or attack that moral in a 1-minute mini-speech. Repeat weekly with new fables.
setup: a book or website of fables
origin: classical progymnasmata (Aphthonius, Hermogenes; Greco-Roman rhetorical education)
variations: Tell the fable from a different character's viewpoint; modernize the setting

name: Chreia Elaboration (Progymnasmata III)
description: Take a famous saying or anecdote and amplify it through the ancient eight-part structure. Trains systematic development of a single idea into a full speech - the original 'speech skeleton' drill.
instructions: Pick a quotable saying or anecdote (e.g., 'Isocrates said the root of education is bitter but the fruit is sweet'). Deliver a short speech with the classical eight parts in order: 1) Praise the author of the saying. 2) Paraphrase the saying in your own words. 3) Give the cause/rationale - why it is true. 4) State the contrary - what happens when it's ignored. 5) Offer a comparison/analogy. 6) Give an example from history or life. 7) Cite a testimony - another authority who agrees. 8) Close with a brief epilogue urging the audience to heed it. Practice until you can run the structure on any quote in 3-4 minutes impromptu.
variations: Proverb (gnome) version uses an anonymous maxim instead of an attributed saying

name: Encomium and Invective (Progymnasmata VIII-IX)
description: Compose and deliver a structured speech of praise (encomium) - then one of blame (invective) - on a person, thing, or idea. The ancestor of every toast, eulogy, and roast.
instructions: 1) Choose a subject: a person, animal, virtue, even a mundane object (praising a humble object is great practice). 2) Build the speech on the classical heads: origin/background; upbringing/education; deeds and qualities (the core - group by virtues: wisdom, courage, justice, self-control); comparison with someone/something lesser; conclusion/exhortation. 3) Deliver it for 3-5 minutes. 4) Then flip: deliver an invective on the same subject using the same heads negatively. 5) Note how the same facts can be framed both ways.
variations: Mock encomium of a trivial object (in praise of the paperclip) for humor training

name: Refutation and Confirmation (Progymnasmata V-VI)
description: Argue that a given story or claim is implausible, then argue the opposite case for the same story. Trains two-sided argument fluency.
instructions: 1) Take a narrative or claim (classically a myth; practically, any news story or popular belief). 2) REFUTE it through the standard heads: it is unclear, implausible, impossible, inconsistent, unfitting, or inexpedient - give a short speech attacking it point by point. 3) Then CONFIRM the same story using the mirrored heads: clear, plausible, possible, consistent, fitting, expedient. 4) Deliver both speeches back-to-back; have a listener judge which was more convincing and why.
variations: Use modern claims (e.g., 'remote work is better') instead of myths

name: Ethopoeia (Character Speech)
description: Deliver the speech a specific character would give at a specific dramatic moment ('What would Achilles say over the body of Patroclus?'). Trains emotional range, perspective-taking, and pathos.
instructions: 1) Pick a character (historical, fictional, or a type: 'a farmer seeing the ocean for the first time') and a charged moment. 2) Compose/improvise their speech in first person, moving through the classical time structure: present circumstances, the past that led here, the future they face. 3) Deliver it with the voice, emotion, and rhythm fitting the character. 4) Repeat with a contrasting character to stretch range.
variations: Historical Figures variant: speak AS a historical object or place ('Mr. U.S. flag, how did you feel...')

name: Ekphrasis (Vivid Description Drill)
description: Describe a scene, object, or event so vividly the audience 'sees' it. The classical training for sensory, concrete language in speeches.
instructions: 1) Choose a subject: a painting, photo, room, or remembered event. 2) Speak for 2-3 minutes making listeners see it: move systematically (top to bottom, outside in, or chronologically for events), engage at least three senses, and use specific nouns over adjectives. 3) Test: a listener who hasn't seen the subject sketches or summarizes it back; gaps show where your description failed. 4) Redo the description fixing the gaps.
setup: an image or scene to describe
variations: The Blank Screen variant: narrate an imaginary slideshow with a clicker (see Blank Screen exercise)

name: Thesis Defense (Progymnasmata XIII)
description: Argue a general question ('Should one marry?', 'Is the city better than the country?') considering and answering objections. Trains structured deliberative speech.
instructions: 1) Pick a general (not personal) question with two defensible sides. 2) Outline: introduction, your thesis, 2-3 arguments from justice/expediency/possibility/honor, then RAISE the strongest objection yourself and answer it, then conclude. 3) Deliver in 3-5 minutes. 4) Have a partner supply one extra objection live, which you must answer impromptu before concluding.
variations: Law variant (nomou eisphora): argue for/against a proposed law

name: Magic Bag Object Speech
description: Pull an everyday object from a bag and immediately tell the group everything you can about it for one minute. Entry-level extemporaneous speaking.
instructions: 1) Fill a bag with everyday items (flashlight, band-aid, paper clip, toothbrush) - more items than speakers. 2) Speaker draws without peeking, stands, and speaks up to one minute about the object: what it is, uses, a story, a sales pitch. 3) Hold your item until everyone has gone so no object repeats. 4) Debrief: which items were hard and why? Would 2 minutes of notes have helped?
origin: 4-H public speaking curriculum ('Demon Destroyer Ideas', University of Idaho Extension)
variations: Solo: grab any household object, set 2-3 minute timer, deliver a cohesive speech about it

name: Make a Commercial
description: Teams invent and perform a 30-60 second TV commercial for a random household item. Trains persuasion, hooks, and enthusiasm on command.
instructions: 1) Discuss what makes commercials memorable (jingle, story, pizazz). 2) Pairs draw an item from a bag (toothbrush, broom, candy). 3) 5-10 minutes to create a TV/radio commercial: hook, product benefits, call to action. 4) Each team performs on a designated 'studio stage'; audience gives positive feedback. 5) Optional: switch items and improvise a commercial with zero prep.
variations: Solo no-prep version: 60-second infomercial for the nearest object, recorded

name: The Blank Screen (Imaginary Slideshow)
description: Narrate a personal memory as an imaginary slide show, 'clicking' through mental pictures. Speakers get lost in description and forget to be nervous.
instructions: 1) Stand at a blank wall or screen with a clicker (or say 'click'). 2) Choose a REAL personal memory: a trip, an embarrassing moment, the place you grew up. 3) Present it as slides: describe the first mental picture in concrete visual detail, 'click', describe the next, and so on for 5-8 slides. 4) End on the slide that carries the point or feeling. 5) Group version: leader demonstrates first, then volunteers show their 'slide sets'.
variations: Photo version: present a real unfamiliar photo and tell its story

name: Back to Back (Pro/Con Ping-Pong)
description: Two speakers sit back to back; one argues only positives of a topic, the other only negatives, alternating. Beginner debate and reframing practice.
instructions: 1) Pair sits or stands back to back. 2) Assign a topic (going to college, getting a job, trying out for a play). 3) One partner is 'positive', the other 'negative'. 4) Alternate 20-30 second turns: positive point, then negative point, back and forth for 4-6 exchanges. 5) Always start and end with the positive speaker. 6) Swap roles with a new topic.
variations: Devil's advocate solo version: argue pro for 60s then con for 60s on a timer

name: Solve the Problem (Balloon Pop Scenarios)
description: Pop a balloon containing a sticky social scenario and explain aloud how you would handle it. Trains poised problem-talk under surprise.
instructions: 1) Write problem situations on slips ('While introducing the keynote speaker, you forget his name'; 'You rip your pants at an away game'). 2) Seal each slip in a balloon, inflate. 3) Speaker pops a balloon, reads the problem aloud, and speaks 1-2 minutes on how they'd handle it. 4) Debrief on quick decision-making.
origin: 4-H curriculum (Public Speaking...4-H Style, Texas Ag Extension)
variations: Pop It variant: balloons contain simple topics instead of problems

name: A to Z Speeches
description: Draw a letter of the alphabet and give a one-minute talk on anything beginning with that letter, after brief prep. Trains topic selection and quick outlining.
instructions: 1) Put letters A-Z on slips. 2) Each speaker draws a letter and gets up to 10 minutes (or 1 minute, for a harder version) to choose a topic starting with that letter and sketch a mini-outline. 3) Deliver a one-minute talk with a beginning, middle, and end. 4) Keep a dictionary handy for desperate letters like Q and X.
origin: 4-H curriculum (Public Speaking...4-H Style, Texas Ag Extension)
variations: No-prep version; or sequence: speak through A to Z in one continuous speech, one sentence per letter

name: Emotion Skits / Emotional Readings
aliases: Mary Had a Little Lamb emotions
description: Deliver the same neutral text in randomly drawn emotions while others guess the emotion. Trains vocal expression and congruence between voice and meaning.
instructions: 1) Leader reads a passage twice: once monotone, once with full expression; group discusses the difference. 2) Put emotion words in a bag (angry, lovestruck, suspicious, exhausted, jealous). 3) Each speaker/pair draws one and delivers a short set piece - a nursery rhyme like 'Mary Had a Little Lamb' or a 3-4 sentence skit - saturated with that emotion. 4) The group guesses the emotion. 5) Re-run with the same text and a different emotion to feel the contrast.
setup: emotion word slips, a short text
variations: Solo: record your speech opening in 6 different emotions (happy, bored, sad, angry, teasing, cynical) and compare

name: Poem Interpretation (Expressive Reading)
description: Prepare and perform a short poem with maximum vocal expression, introduced formally. Trains projection, expression, and performing prepared text.
instructions: 1) Each speaker gets a short, vivid poem (Shel Silverstein works well). 2) Practice with a partner for a few minutes, marking words to stress and places to pause. 3) Come to the front and introduce it: '[Title] by [author], interpreted by [name]'. 4) Read with as much expression as the text allows; show the illustration if there is one. 5) Group discusses which interpretations landed; volunteers re-interpret the same poem differently.
variations: Solo daily read-aloud: one poem a day recorded, listening back for monotone patches

name: On-the-Spot Presentation Introductions
description: Craft and deliver only the INTRODUCTION to an imaginary how-to presentation, competing to hook the audience. Isolates and trains openings.
instructions: 1) Prepare topic cards with trivially simple how-tos ('how to tie your shoe', 'how to sit in a chair'). 2) Demonstrate a flat opening vs. a dramatic story-based opening for the same topic. 3) Each speaker draws a card and gets 5-10 minutes to craft just an opening: a story, question, startling claim, or scene that makes the mundane topic urgent. 4) Deliver openings one after another; group votes on which hooked them most and names why.
variations: Same drill for closings: deliver only the final 30 seconds of an imaginary speech

name: Character Interviews (Pretend Press)
description: One partner invents a character, the other interviews them news-style in front of the group. Trains Q&A poise, microphone skills, and staying in role.
instructions: 1) Pairs: one is a news reporter, one creates a 'character' (props/hats optional, or assigned characters like Pinocchio or the Queen). 2) 10-15 minutes prep with a stock interview script: introduction, 'how long have you lived in...', 'tell us what you do', plus invented questions. 3) Perform the interview at the front with a pretend (or real) microphone. 4) Switch roles in a later round. 5) Optionally videotape and review projection, audience-facing, and fidgets.
setup: interview question sheets; optional props and microphone
variations: Hostile-press version for advanced: interviewer asks pointed gotcha questions

name: Noodle Game (Convince Me It's Not a Noodle)
description: Pass an object around a circle; each person loudly and convincingly declares it to be something it is not. Trains projection, conviction, and commitment.
instructions: 1) Group stands in a circle with one object (half a foam pool noodle is classic). 2) Leader holds it up and declares in a loud, emphatic voice: 'This is not a noodle, it is a puppy dog!' with full conviction. 3) Pass to the next person who denies the previous claim and asserts a new one: 'This is not a puppy dog, it is a ____!' 4) Continue around; the only rule is total vocal commitment - loud, expressive, convincing. Object cannot be a person.
origin: Cindy Osterlund, Oregon State University Extension (Fun with Speaking)
variations: Sell-it version: each holder gives a 15-second sales pitch for the imaginary object

name: Speech Fear Snowball Fight
description: Write your speaking fears anonymously, crumple them into 'snowballs', throw them, then read and discuss someone else's fear aloud. Normalizes anxiety before speaking practice.
instructions: 1) Everyone writes their fears/hesitations about public speaking on paper, anonymously. 2) Crumple into balls and have a 30-second 'snowball fight'. 3) Each person picks up a nearby snowball and reads the fear aloud to the group. 4) Group briefly discusses: who shares this fear? what helps? 5) Proceed into a low-stakes speaking game while the lesson - everyone is nervous - is fresh.

name: Diaphragmatic Breathing for Speakers
description: Structured breathing practice that builds breath support and downshifts pre-speech nerves. The standard pre-talk warmup.
instructions: 1) Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, shoulders and stomach relaxed, hands on belly. 2) Inhale through the nose for a count of 4, feeling the belly (not chest) expand. 3) Exhale through the mouth for 4. 4) Repeat several rounds, gradually extending to counts of 8-10. 5) Use 4-6 rounds in the minutes before any speech; practice daily so it's automatic under nerves.
variations: Box breathing (4-4-4-4); exhale on a hiss to a count of 20 for breath-support strength

name: Speech Rate Stretch
description: Deliver the same minute of your speech at exaggeratedly slow and fast rates to gain conscious control of pace.
instructions: 1) Record one minute of your speech at your normal rate. 2) Re-record it very slow - stretching every phrase. 3) Re-record it very fast but still articulate. 4) Listen to all three: where does slow add weight? Where does fast add energy? 5) Deliver a final version deliberately varying rate by content: slow for key claims, faster for lists and asides. Mark rate changes in your notes.
variations: Metronome version: speak to 100, then 160 bpm; pause drill: insert a full 2-second pause after every key sentence

name: Tongue Twister Progression
description: Daily tongue twisters spoken slowly then accelerated, keeping every consonant crisp. The standard articulation warmup before speaking.
instructions: 1) Pick 2-3 twisters ('red leather, yellow leather'; 'unique New York'; 'the lips, the teeth, the tip of the tongue'). 2) Say each slowly with exaggerated mouth movement, every sound crisp. 3) Repeat, increasing speed only while clarity holds; drop back when it smears. 4) Do 5 minutes daily for two weeks; rotate twisters targeting your problem sounds. 5) Use 60 seconds of twisters as a pre-speech warmup.
origin: theatre/speech pedagogy; NSDA lesson plans time twisters at 15 seconds
variations: Pencil-in-teeth version (speak a passage with a pencil between teeth, then without); race format in groups

name: Video Self-Review
description: Record a full run of your talk and review it like a coach, with a structured checklist. The highest-leverage feedback loop available alone.
instructions: 1) Set up a phone at audience eye level; record a full delivery of your talk standing, as if live. 2) Watch once for content: structure, clarity, length. 3) Watch again muted: posture, gestures, eye line, fidgets. 4) Listen once audio-only: fillers, pace, monotone patches, mumbled spots. 5) Write down exactly 3 things to change; re-record. Keep recordings to compare across weeks.
origin: universal speaker training; codified in coaching write-ups
variations: Audio-only walk-and-talk review; watch at 2x to make gesture patterns obvious

name: Enthusiasm Transplant
description: Speak about something you feel nothing about as if it thrills you. Trains the energy and animation that audiences read as charisma.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic you're indifferent to (lint, tax forms, gravel). 2) Speak for 1-2 minutes about it with full contagious enthusiasm: energized voice, big gestures, delighted facial expression, superlatives. 3) Record and watch: does it read as genuine? 4) Note which physical choices created the energy; consciously reuse them on your real material. 5) Repeat with topics of mild interest, transferring the same animation.
variations: Dial version: deliver the same passage at enthusiasm levels 2, 5, 8, and 10 to calibrate

name: Eye Contact Sweep Practice
description: Deliberately practice holding 3-5 seconds of eye contact per person, distributed across all zones of the room, while speaking.
instructions: 1) In any group speaking chance (meeting, class, club), pick 5 anchor people: front, back, left, right, middle. 2) While speaking, hold each person's eyes for a full thought (3-5 seconds) - long enough to register connection, not a stare - then move to another zone, unpredictably rather than in a mechanical sweep. 3) Solo practice: place 5 sticky notes with drawn faces around the room at head height and deliver your talk making 'eye contact' with each in turn. 4) Video-check: does your eye line favor one side or the floor?
variations: One-sentence-one-person rule: complete exactly one sentence per person before moving

name: PREP Framework Daily Reps
description: Daily practice answering random questions aloud using the PREP structure (Point, Reason, Example, Point) until the framework becomes automatic.
instructions: 1) Each day, pick one random question from an online list (or have someone ask you one). 2) Answer aloud in PREP order: state your Point first ('I believe X'), give your Reason ('because...'), give one concrete Example or piece of evidence, then restate your Point as the close. 3) Keep it to 60-90 seconds. 4) Do this daily for a month; the structure becomes automatic and your thinking shifts entirely to content. 5) Then deploy it live in meetings and Q&A.
origin: business communication training; widely taught in Toastmasters and corporate coaching
variations: Swap frameworks weekly: Past-Present-Future; Problem-Solution-Benefit; Point-Story-Point

name: Murder Board (Adversarial Q&A Rehearsal)
description: A panel of colleagues role-plays a hostile audience, grilling you after your presentation with incisive, rapid-fire, and gotcha questions. The gold standard for Q&A and high-stakes prep.
instructions: 1) Recruit 2-5 people; brief them on your audience and ask them to role-play specific stakeholders (skeptical exec, hostile journalist, pedantic expert). 2) Deliver your full talk or opening statement, timed. 3) Panel attacks: devil's-advocate challenges, what-if scenarios, interruptions, rapid-fire questions, attacks on assumptions. 4) You practice the discipline: pause, restate or bridge the question, answer concisely, return to message. 5) Debrief: list every question you handled badly, script better answers, and re-run the worst five. Repeat until nothing surprises you.
origin: U.S. Army instructor training; standard in political debate prep and proposal orals coaching
variations: Solo-lite: write the 10 hardest questions you fear, record yourself answering each cold

name: Full Extemp Practice Round
description: Simulate a complete extemporaneous speaking round: draw a current-events question, prep 30 minutes with sources, deliver a 7-minute speech without notes. The 'drill to end all drills' for structured speaking.
instructions: 1) Get practice questions (NSDA publishes monthly extemp question sets; or write your own from this week's news). 2) Draw three questions, pick one. 3) Start a 30-minute prep timer: research with whatever files/articles you allow yourself, outline an intro, 2-3 structured points with cited evidence, and a conclusion that answers the question. 4) Deliver 7 minutes, no notes (or one notecard), in front of someone - or taped if alone. 5) Review against: did you actually answer the question? Was each point supported?
variations: Compress prep to 15 then 5 minutes as you improve; Table-Topics-ify it with 0 prep for 2 minutes

name: Concept Teach-Back Drill
description: Mine an article for every concept it references, research each briefly, then deliver a one-minute explainer speech on each. Trains the explanatory clarity that underpins persuasive speaking.
instructions: 1) Take one substantive news article. 2) List every concept it assumes you know (e.g., 'tariff', 'coalition government', 'bond yield'). 3) Spend 10 minutes researching each. 4) For each concept, deliver a one-minute speech explaining it to an imagined smart 12-year-old: definition, why it matters, one example. 5) Record one and check for jargon leaks.
origin: NSDA Extemp Skills and Drills (Ethan Reeves)
variations: Country/state version: name 5 facts about a random country off the top of your head, then learn 5 more

name: Three Futures Analysis Speech
description: Pick a current event, generate three possible future scenarios aloud, and argue which is most probable. Trains the analytical depth that separates good speakers from word-fillers.
instructions: 1) Pick a developing news story. 2) Speak through three plausible future scenarios for it. 3) For each: identify the variables that would drive it and assess its probability. 4) Conclude by committing to the most likely outcome and defending that judgment. 5) Bonus calibration: note your prediction and check back in a month.
origin: NSDA Extemp Skills and Drills (Ethan Reeves)
variations: Disagree drill: find an opinion article, deliver a speech arguing against its stance with reasoning and evidence

name: Rewind (Impromptu Redo)
description: Give an impromptu speech, then immediately give a better one on the same topic after two minutes of reflection. Trains self-diagnosis and shows you the gap between first and second drafts of your thinking.
instructions: 1) Draw a topic and deliver an impromptu speech (1-3 minutes). 2) Take exactly 2 minutes to identify what went wrong: weak structure? thin examples? rambling ending? 3) Deliver the speech again on the same topic, fixing those specific flaws. 4) Note which fixes recur across sessions - those are your systematic weaknesses.
origin: speech & debate coaching (Danielle Miller impromptu drills)
variations: Prep-only second round: outline the redo but don't deliver it

name: Hand Signals Live Coaching
description: A helper flashes pre-agreed hand signals during your speech (louder, slow down, more passion, move), and you adjust in real time without stopping. Trains mid-speech self-correction.
instructions: 1) With a partner, agree on 3-4 signals targeting YOUR weaknesses: palm up = volume, slow wave = pace down, fist = more energy, walk fingers = move/gesture. 2) Deliver a 3-5 minute speech (prepared or impromptu). 3) Partner flashes signals whenever needed; you must comply within one sentence without breaking flow. 4) Debrief which adjustments felt hardest. 5) Swap roles.
origin: speech & debate coaching (Danielle Miller impromptu drills)
variations: Dynamics version: partner holds up 1-10 fingers and you scale volume/pace/energy to that number continuously

name: Three Stories Pocket Drill
description: Pre-load three diverse personal stories, then force one to fit whatever random topic you draw. Trains the universal speaker skill of adapting existing material to any prompt.
instructions: 1) Write three diverse stories from your life on a sticky note (one-line titles: 'lost luggage in Rome', 'first job firing', 'dog ate the cake'). 2) Draw a random impromptu topic. 3) During 1-2 minutes prep, find the angle by which one of your three stories illustrates the topic. 4) Deliver a speech whose body is that story, framed to the topic. 5) Repeat with new topics until each story has been bent to fit at least 3 unrelated prompts.
variations: Build a 10-story bank over time; require a different story each round

name: Counting Down (Speak to the Timer)
description: Set a countdown for your goal duration and keep speaking until it hits zero, even through pauses and blanks. Stretches your capacity to fill time gracefully.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic, set a visible countdown (start 2 minutes, grow to 5). 2) Speak until the timer expires. Pausing to think is allowed; stopping is not. 3) When you blank, use rescue moves aloud: restate your point another way, add an example, zoom out to why it matters, preview your next point. 4) Track how often you needed rescues; watch the number fall across sessions.
origin: speech & debate coaching (Danielle Miller impromptu drills)
variations: Sectioned version: split the countdown into intro/3 points/conclusion with sub-timers and move on when each expires

name: Odd Topics Persuasion
description: Deliver a genuinely persuasive, emotionally resonant speech about something trivial (beige, kittens, Christmas lights), usually via analogy. Trains finding significance anywhere.
instructions: 1) Draw a deliberately mundane topic. 2) Take 2 minutes prep to find the bigger meaning - usually an analogy ('beige is the color of compromise...'). 3) Deliver a 2-3 minute speech with full conviction, real structure, and an emotional appeal, treating the topic as profound. 4) A listener rates whether the speech achieved actual impact or stayed jokey. The goal is sincerity, not parody.
variations: Mock-epic version played for laughs (overlaps with mock encomium)

name: Newspaper Floor Drill (Anti-Pacing)
description: Rehearse standing on spread-out newspaper; every unintentional shuffle, rock, or sway crunches audibly. Builds stillness and makes movement deliberate.
instructions: 1) Spread newspaper sheets (or bubble wrap for stronger feedback) where you'll stand. 2) Deliver your talk. Every crunch is a step you didn't plan. 3) Allowed: deliberate steps forward to emphasize, steps back to signal transitions - take them cleanly and re-plant. 4) Goal: a full run where every sound underfoot was intentional. 5) Then rehearse once off the paper and notice your new groundedness.
variations: Stage-zones version: tape 3 floor zones and assign each section of your talk to one, moving only at transitions

name: Table Read (Seated Script Pass)
description: Read your full talk aloud seated, with a listener, purely for structure, flow, language, and timing - before any staging work. The first rehearsal layer used by TED coaches.
instructions: 1) Sit at a table with your script or detailed outline; a partner (or recorder) listens. 2) Read the entire talk aloud at performance pace - no acting, no gestures. 3) Mark every place you stumble, every sentence that reads as 'written' rather than spoken, and every section that drags. 4) Time it; note benchmark timestamps (where you should be at each third). 5) Rewrite spoken-awkward passages into spoken English and re-read. Only then move to standing rehearsal.
variations: Solo: record the read and listen on a walk; benchmark timing version for long talks (know your 6/12/18-minute marks)

name: Memory Layering Rehearsal
description: Rehearse your talk through different modalities - writing, listening, walking, visualizing - to build multiple retrieval pathways so you can't blank on stage.
instructions: 1) Write your talk outline by hand from memory. 2) Record the talk and listen during commutes. 3) Deliver it aloud while walking (kinesthetic). 4) Visualize delivering it: see the room, feel the clicker, hear your opening line. 5) Do a 'keyword run': deliver the talk from a 10-word skeleton only. 6) Final test: have someone name any section and deliver it cold from that point.
variations: Start-anywhere drill: shuffle section cards and deliver in random order

name: Mirror Gesture Sync
description: Rehearse key lines in front of a mirror, deliberately timing broad gestures to land on the words they emphasize. Builds a natural-looking gesture vocabulary.
instructions: 1) Pick 5 key sentences from your talk. 2) For each, choose one purposeful gesture: pointing, painting a picture, counting on fingers, 'setting the ball down' on the key word, opening palms. 3) In a mirror, deliver each line timing the gesture's peak to the stressed word. 4) Gestures originate from the core, travel outside the body silhouette, then hands return calmly to your sides - no fig-leaf clasp, no pockets. 5) Run the lines twice: once with NO gestures (to feel the baseline), once with the planned ones. 6) Video-check that nothing repeats mechanically.
variations: Hands-pinned round: deliver with hands clasped behind back to feel how much your voice must carry, then release

name: Walk to the Front
description: Practice only the first ten seconds: walk up, plant, pause, acknowledge the audience, say one line, and walk back. Trains the composed entrance that sets the tone for a whole talk.
instructions: 1) Group lines up single file. 2) One at a time: walk to center front unhurried, land with feet planted shoulder-width and hands at sides, PAUSE a full beat, sweep eyes across the audience, smile, say 'hello' or your prepared opening line with one gesture, pause again, walk back. 3) Coach calls re-dos for rushed landings, skipped pauses, or hands that fidget. 4) Repeat until the pause before speaking feels owned, not endured.
origin: The Practice Space presentation drills; also a 4-H 'Silent Speakers' exercise
variations: Silent Speakers: walk up, make eye contact with everyone, smile, walk back - no words at all

name: Contrasting Colors (Vocal Color Drill)
description: Deliver the same lines in distinct vocal 'colors' (passionate red, urgent gray, calm blue, breezy green, kind orange) and have listeners guess the color. Expands tonal range and control.
instructions: 1) Choose 2-4 lines from any text. 2) Read them flat once as a baseline. 3) Re-deliver in each color: red = passionate/excited; gray = urgent/forceful; blue = serious/calm; green = breezy/conversational; orange = kind/encouraging. 4) Practice switching color mid-passage on a partner's snap. 5) Partner guesses which color you intended; misses show where your range collapses. 6) Apply: mark your real talk with color shifts per section.
variations: Emotion version with feelings instead of colors; conduct a partner like an orchestra raising/lowering intensity

name: Confidence Contest
description: Pass an identical opinion statement around a circle, each person delivering it more confidently than the last. Isolates and escalates the components of confident delivery.
instructions: 1) Sit in a circle. 2) First person states an opinion with reasons ('Blueberries are the best fruit because they're delicious and full of antioxidants'). 3) The next person repeats the exact words but MORE confidently: stronger volume, steadier eye contact, downward inflection at sentence ends, expressive face. 4) Continue through four people, then start a new statement. 5) Debrief: name concretely what changed between round 1 and round 4.
variations: Solo: record the same sentence at confidence levels 3, 6, and 10 and compare

name: Paraphrase It
description: Open a random page of any book and immediately re-explain its content aloud in your own words, then again in the fewest words possible. Trains speaking-from-notes and concision.
instructions: 1) Open any book to a random page; read a paragraph. 2) Without re-reading, explain its content aloud in your own words. 3) Do a second pass: same content in the FEWEST possible words with zero filler. 4) Record occasionally and listen for distracting verbal habits. 5) This simulates glancing at notes and speaking naturally rather than reading.
variations: Article version: after daily news reading, deliver a short spoken summary (extemp habit-stack)

name: Tell Me About a Time (Eye Contact Stories)
description: Tell a 2-minute personal memory triggered by a sensory prompt (cold, rain, losing track of time) while keeping natural eye contact; partner gives feedback on connection.
instructions: 1) Partner offers a concrete prompt: 'tell me about a time you were freezing', '...you got lost', '...you lost track of time'. 2) Speaker tells the 2-minute memory aiming for genuine eye contact and emotional truth rather than polish. 3) Listener gives feedback ONLY on connection: when did eye contact feel natural vs. forced? when did emotion land? 4) Swap roles, new prompt.

name: Pre-Speech Physical Warmup Sequence
description: A 5-minute full-body routine (tension scan, rolls, stretches, shake-out, energizers) that converts pre-talk anxiety into relaxed energy.
instructions: 1) Eyes closed, breathe deep, scan for tension spots. 2) Roll shoulders, neck, wrists, ankles. 3) Reach high, middle, low; roll up the spine slowly. 4) Bounce with loose knees; shake out arms and legs. 5) Face stretch: alternate stretching the face wide open and scrunching it tight. 6) Whole-body tense-and-release. 7) Finish with 20 seconds of jumping jacks or running in place for alert energy. Do the full sequence before every talk and before practice sessions.
origin: theatre warmup tradition via The Practice Space
variations: Add the vocal warmup stack: sighs high-to-low, lip trills, tongue trills, hum-to-yawn

name: Demosthenes Noise Training
description: Practice delivering your speech over loud ambient noise (the modern version of Demosthenes shouting over waves) to build projection and breath power.
instructions: 1) Play loud ambient noise (crowd noise, traffic recording, or practice outdoors near real noise) at a level that would drown out conversational speech. 2) Deliver your speech so an imagined listener 10 meters away over the noise would hear every word - power from breath support, not throat strain (stop if your throat hurts). 3) 5 minutes max per session. 4) Then deliver one minute in a silent room and notice the effortless reserve of power.
setup: noise source or noisy outdoor spot
origin: Demosthenes' training as told by Plutarch; adapted in modern voice coaching
variations: Recite-while-running version (Demosthenes recited verses uphill) for breath control under exertion

name: Pencil Articulation Drill
description: Speak a passage with a pencil or wine cork held gently between your teeth, then remove it - articulation snaps into over-clarity. The safe modern descendant of Demosthenes' pebbles.
instructions: 1) Hold a pencil or cork lightly between your front teeth. 2) Read a paragraph or your speech opening aloud, working lips and tongue hard to be understood around the obstruction, 2-3 minutes. 3) Remove it and read the same passage: enunciation will feel effortless and crisp. 4) Use before talks and daily during an articulation-improvement block. (Never use small objects like actual pebbles - choking hazard.)
origin: Demosthenes legend; standard actor/broadcaster warmup adaptation
variations: Over-articulation drill: read exaggerating every consonant to absurdity, then dial back to normal

name: Toast Practice Protocol
description: A structured way to write and rehearse a short occasion speech (toast, tribute, eulogy): draft on a proven frame, then graduated rehearsal from page to memory to audience.
instructions: 1) Draft 2-3 minutes on the standard frame: who you are and your connection; one specific story that shows the honoree's character (not a resume, not an inside joke); what that story means; raise-the-glass line. 2) Read it aloud off the page 3 times, editing anything your mouth stumbles on. 3) Recite from bullet points only; then with no notes. 4) Record once and listen on commutes to internalize. 5) Deliver to one trusted listener for feedback on warmth and length. 6) Final dress run holding a real glass, including the physical raise.
origin: wedding/eulogy speaking guidance distilled from etiquette and speech coaching write-ups
variations: Practice version with fictional honorees: toast a friend's imaginary retirement as a drill

name: Elevator Pitch Reps
description: Craft and repeatedly deliver a 30-60 second pitch (of yourself, your project, or an idea), tightening it across reps and audiences. Core persuasion-in-miniature practice.
instructions: 1) Write the pitch: hook question or surprising fact; what you do/propose in one plain sentence; why it matters to THIS listener; a concrete ask or next step. 2) Deliver it to a timer at 60s, then cut to 30s. 3) Record both; cut every word that doesn't earn its place. 4) Deliver to 3 different people, adjusting the 'why it matters' line to each. 5) Re-test cold a week later - if you can't deliver it on demand, it isn't done.
origin: business communication / workshop staple (SessionLab et al.)
variations: Pitch ordinary objects for practice; 'pitch ladder': same idea at 10s, 30s, 2min versions

name: Fear Ladder for Speaking (Exposure Hierarchy)
description: Build a personal 8-10 rung ladder of increasingly scary speaking situations and climb it systematically, repeating each rung until anxiety drops. The CBT-backed cure for speaking dread.
instructions: 1) List speaking situations from least to most scary, rated 0-100 anxiety. Example rungs: read aloud alone; record your voice and listen back; speak to a mirror; deliver to one trusted friend; speak on a video call; ask a question at a meeting; give a 2-minute update to your team; attend a Toastmasters meeting and do Table Topics; give a prepared talk to 10+; volunteer for a Q&A-heavy slot. 2) Start at a rung rated ~40. 3) Repeat that exposure 3-5 times across days until anxiety drops noticeably before/while doing it. 4) Move up one rung. Practice 3-5 times per week; never skip more than one rung. 5) Pair with slow breathing; do NOT use safety crutches (reading verbatim, avoiding eye contact) - they block the learning.
setup: written ladder; willing micro-audiences for upper rungs
origin: CBT exposure therapy applied to public speaking fear
variations: Imaginal first pass: vividly visualize each rung before doing it live

name: 4-Point Refutation Drill
description: Take a single opposing argument, prep briefly, then deliver a rebuttal that runs the full four-part refutation structure: identify, tag, support, impact. The core debate drill for organized, repeatable rebuttals.
instructions: 1) Pull one argument from a sourcebook, sample case, or just invent a claim ('social media should be banned for under-16s'). 2) Give yourself prep time (60 seconds for beginners, less as you improve). 3) Deliver your rebuttal in four labeled moves: IDENTIFY the argument you're answering ('On my opponent's claim that...'); TAG your response with a short headline ('This ignores enforcement costs'); SUPPORT with logic and evidence; IMPACT - explain why your point wins and why it matters. 4) Repeat with a new argument; do 5-10 in a row. 5) Optionally record one and check that all four parts were clearly present.
setup: list of arguments or claims, timer
variations: Set a minimum time you must fill, or a maximum you can't exceed, to train length control

name: Speed/Spreading Reading Drill
description: Read text aloud as fast as you possibly can while keeping every word articulate, for an extended stretch. Builds vocal fluency, breath stamina, and clarity at speed used by competitive debaters.
instructions: 1) Get any dense text (an article, a debate case, a book page). 2) Read it aloud as fast as you can for up to 20 minutes, keeping your mouth wide open and tongue unrestrained so words stay crisp - never let speed smear the words. 3) Partner version: a listener tries to 'flow' (note tags, names, dates, key claims) and calls 'clear!' whenever your delivery becomes unintelligible, forcing you to re-articulate. 4) Stop if your throat strains; power should come from breath, not the throat. 5) Afterward, read at normal pace and notice the new ease and precision.
variations: Backwards-words version (read sentences word-by-word in reverse) to force articulation over autopilot; pen-in-mouth combo

name: Translation Drill (Jargon to Lay)
description: Deliver a technical speech and, on a partner's cue, instantly switch from jargon-heavy language into plain language a layperson would understand, then back again. Trains audience adaptation in real time.
instructions: 1) Prepare or improvise a speech full of technical/specialist language on a topic you know. 2) Begin delivering it. 3) Every 10-40 seconds your partner calls 'translate!' - you must immediately re-explain what you just said in plain, jargon-free language a smart 12-year-old or non-expert would follow. 4) When they call 'translate' again, switch back to the technical register. 5) Keep alternating for 3-5 minutes; swap roles. The goal is fluent code-switching between expert and lay audiences.
setup: a topic you can speak on technically; a partner
variations: Solo: deliver a passage technically, then re-deliver entirely in plain English; record both

name: PechaKucha (20x20)
description: Deliver a talk over exactly 20 slides that auto-advance every 20 seconds (6 min 40 sec total). The relentless auto-advance forces tight pacing, rehearsal, and a clean narrative arc.
instructions: 1) Build (or download) a deck of 20 image-led slides on a topic or story. 2) Set the slides to auto-advance every 20 seconds - you cannot click; they move whether you're ready or not. 3) Script and rehearse roughly 20 seconds of narration per slide, with smooth transitions and a through-line connecting all 20. 4) Deliver the full 6:40 standing, keeping pace with the slides exactly. 5) Review where you fell behind or rushed; re-rehearse those slides. Ignite variant: 20 slides at 15 seconds each (5 minutes).
setup: slide software with auto-advance timing; projector optional
origin: Klein-Dytham Architecture, Tokyo (2003); Ignite created by O'Reilly Media
variations: Group 'PechaKucha night' where each person presents one deck; image-only decks of someone else's photos for impromptu narration

name: Just A Minute
description: Speak for 60 seconds on a surprise topic without hesitation, repetition, or deviation, while opponents buzz in to challenge any slip. A classic BBC radio game that builds fluency and composure under interruption.
instructions: 1) One player is given a random subject and must talk about it for 60 seconds. 2) Three rules: no HESITATION (no pauses or filled 'um'), no REPETITION (don't repeat a significant word/phrase), no DEVIATION (stay on topic and on coherent English). 3) Other players listen and buzz/shout to challenge any infraction. 4) If the challenge is correct, the challenger takes over the topic for the remaining time; if wrong, the speaker keeps going. 5) Whoever is speaking when the minute ends scores a point. Rotate subjects.
setup: list of topics, a timer, a buzzer or 'stop' signal
origin: BBC Radio 4 panel game 'Just a Minute' (Ian Messiter, 1967); widely adapted in classrooms and Toastmasters
variations: Solo: speak 60 seconds and self-penalize each filler by restarting; 30-second beginner version

name: Word of the Day Challenge
description: Adopt one new word for a meeting or a day and work it naturally into your speaking. Expands active vocabulary and the agility to deploy precise words live.
instructions: 1) Choose one useful word (adjectives and verbs slot in more easily than nouns), with its part of speech and a model sentence. 2) Post it visibly. 3) During a meeting, conversation, or practice session, everyone tries to use the word - correctly - in their speaking. 4) A designated 'grammarian' notes who used it (and any misuse) and reports at the end. 5) Solo version: pick a word each morning and consciously use it in three real conversations that day.
setup: a chosen word with definition; visible display
origin: Toastmasters meeting roles (Grammarian / Word of the Day)
variations: Forbidden-word inverse: ban a crutch word for a session and have a counter ding every slip

name: Grammarian Listening Role
description: Take the formal role of monitoring everyone's language during a meeting - noting fillers, grammar slips, mispronunciations, vivid phrases, and word-of-the-day use - then deliver a report. Sharpens your ear for the very habits you want to fix in your own speech.
instructions: 1) Volunteer (or assign) the grammarian role for a real or practice meeting. 2) As each person speaks, log: incomplete sentences, grammatical errors, malapropisms, mispronunciations, filler words, and especially vivid/effective language worth praising. 3) Track who uses the word of the day. 4) At the end, deliver a 2-3 minute report: praise the best language used, then note common errors for the group to watch. 5) Rotate the role so everyone trains their critical ear.
setup: notepad; a meeting or group to observe
variations: Ah-Counter role: track only filler words; Timer role: practice precise time-awareness by signaling speakers

name: Monroe's Motivated Sequence Drill
description: Build and deliver a persuasive mini-speech using Monroe's five-step sequence (Attention, Need, Satisfaction, Visualization, Action). Trains the most reliable structure for moving an audience to act.
instructions: 1) Pick something you want to persuade an audience to do (donate, change a habit, adopt a policy). 2) Draft and deliver the speech in five steps: ATTENTION - a hook (startling fact, story, question); NEED - establish the problem and why it matters to them; SATISFACTION - present your solution clearly; VISUALIZATION - paint a vivid picture of life with the solution (and/or without it); ACTION - a specific, concrete call to action. 3) Keep it to 3-5 minutes. 4) Analysis rep: watch an infomercial or campaign ad and label all five steps. 5) Re-deliver, strengthening the weakest step.
variations: Infomercial version: deliver a 60-second mock infomercial hitting all five steps for a random object

name: Impromptu Framework Rotation
description: Answer random prompts aloud using a different impromptu structure each round (Past-Present-Future, What/So What/Now What, Story-Message-Gain, Pro-Con-Conclusion). Builds a toolbox of go-to scaffolds so you're never blank.
instructions: 1) Write the frameworks on cards: PAST-PRESENT-FUTURE (how it was, is, will be); WHAT / SO WHAT / NOW WHAT (the thing, why it matters, what to do); STORY-MESSAGE-GAIN (tell a story, state the lesson, give the takeaway); PRO-CON-CONCLUSION (advantages, disadvantages, your verdict); 5 W's (who/what/when/where/why). 2) Draw a random topic and a random framework card. 3) Deliver a 60-90 second impromptu speech following that exact structure. 4) Re-draw and rotate frameworks. 5) Over weeks, notice which scaffolds fit which topic types so you can pick instantly under pressure.
origin: impromptu speaking pedagogy (Toastmasters, Matt Button, winning-presentations)
variations: Bridging-phrase drill: practice only the time-buying opener ('That's a great question, and it reminds me of...') before launching into a framework

name: Speaking Of... Story Chain
description: Each speaker tells a short true story, and the next person launches their own with 'Speaking of...', linking to something in the prior story. Trains listening, segues, and pulling stories from memory on cue.
instructions: 1) Group sits in a circle; the leader offers a concrete prompt (cold weather, getting lost, a small kindness). 2) First person tells a 1-2 minute true story. 3) The next person must begin 'Speaking of [some element from the last story]...' and tell their own related true story. 4) Continue around the circle, each linking back to the previous tale. 5) Debrief: which segues felt natural, and how did people mine their memory for a matching story?
variations: Pair version trading stories back and forth; require the link to be thematic, not literal

name: Twist It
description: Take an ordinary story prompt and add a surprising twist before telling it ('a time you led' becomes 'a time you led but felt like a fraud'). Trains fresh angles and avoiding cliche.
instructions: 1) Receive a generic prompt: 'tell me about a time you were a leader', 'a proud moment', 'a holiday'. 2) Before speaking, twist it into a less obvious angle: '...but I didn't feel like a leader', '...that I'm secretly not proud of', '...that went completely wrong'. 3) Tell the 2-minute true story from that twisted angle. 4) Work in pairs and swap. 5) Discuss how the twist made the story more interesting than the straight version.
variations: Apply to speech openings: take a stock opener and twist it before delivering

name: What Is Going On? (Photo Inference Story)
description: A group examines a single photo and builds a one-minute story explaining who the people are, what led to this moment, and what happens next. Trains inference, vivid detail, and collaborative narrative.
instructions: 1) Project or pass around an evocative photo (strangers, an odd scene). 2) As a group, interrogate it: What is happening? Who are these people? What evidence in the image supports your guess? What happened just before? What happens next? 3) Synthesize answers into a coherent 1-minute story. 4) Have one person deliver it aloud to the group. 5) Reveal or discuss alternative readings of the same photo.
variations: Solo: pull a random stock photo and narrate its backstory for 90 seconds

name: Three Words Story
description: Brainstorm three unrelated words, then tell a 2-minute story inspired by one of them. Builds the skill of generating material from a tiny, arbitrary seed.
instructions: 1) The group brainstorms three unrelated words - concrete or abstract (e.g., 'lighthouse', 'envy', 'spoon'). 2) Each speaker silently picks ONE of the three and tells a 2-minute story inspired by it - the word can be a subtle theme or a central object, not necessarily named. 3) Don't try to cram all three words; one is enough. 4) Listeners afterward guess which word seeded the story. 5) Re-run with three new words.
variations: Hot Seat combo: audience throws three words and the storyteller must weave a tale using all three

name: What Am I? (Detailed Description Guessing)
description: Describe an object in rich detail without naming it while a listener guesses. Trains precise, vivid, audience-oriented description - the engine of explanation and ekphrasis.
instructions: 1) Pick an object in the room (or, harder, one not visible). 2) Describe it in great sensory and functional detail - shape, color, texture, use, where you'd find it - WITHOUT naming it or any obvious synonym. 3) The listener gets three guesses. 4) If they fail, identify which descriptive details were missing or misleading and redo. 5) Swap roles. Advanced: describe an abstract concept (justice, nostalgia) without using the word.
variations: Twenty-questions inverse where the audience asks yes/no questions to identify your secret object

name: Ordinary Into Extraordinary
description: Tell a true but utterly mundane story (making breakfast, the commute) as if it were dramatic, suspenseful, and gripping. Trains stakes, pacing, and the delivery that makes anything compelling.
instructions: 1) Choose a genuinely boring topic from your day: packing your bag, brushing your teeth, waiting for a bus. 2) Tell it as a 3-minute story dripping with drama, suspense, and significance - building tension, foreshadowing, raising the stakes, using vivid language and vocal dynamics. 3) Stay TRUE to what happened; use exaggeration of tone and framing, not invented facts. 4) Audience rates how gripped they were despite the trivial content. 5) Note which techniques (pauses, stakes, sensory detail) did the heavy lifting.
variations: Overlaps with Odd Topics Persuasion; here the goal is narrative tension rather than persuasion

name: Portraits (Person Description Story)
description: Tell a 2.5-minute true story about a person you've encountered, spending most of it on vivid description, then end by saying why they stuck with you. Trains characterization and sensory detail.
instructions: 1) Pick a real person you've met - memorable, odd, or moving. 2) Tell a 2.5-minute story where the first 1.5+ minutes is pure description: their appearance, the way they spoke, what they wore, how they smelled, how they made you feel. 3) Close with 2-3 sentences on why they're unforgettable. 4) Listeners report what image of the person they now carry. 5) Redo, adding one more vivid concrete detail and cutting one generic one.
variations: Describe a place instead of a person with the same description-then-meaning structure

name: Tour Guide
description: Lead a partner or group around a room as a tour guide, telling a brief story inspired by each object you pass. Trains continuous fluent narration, movement, and spontaneous invention.
instructions: 1) Become a museum/tour guide; your audience follows you around the actual room. 2) Stop at objects one by one - a chair, a window, a coffee mug - and deliver a short, confident, guide-style spiel about each: its history, significance, or a story it inspires (literal or invented). 3) Keep moving and keep talking with smooth transitions between 'exhibits'. 4) Maintain the authoritative, engaging tour-guide energy throughout. 5) Swap and let someone else guide.
variations: Guide a tour of an imaginary place (your dream house, the year 3000)

name: Camp Fire (Audience-Built Story)
description: The audience supplies a main character, a setting, and a problem; the speaker tells a 2-minute fictional story using all three. Low-stakes improvised storytelling under constraints.
instructions: 1) Speaker asks the audience for three things: a main character, a setting, and a problem/conflict. 2) Take a breath and tell a 2-minute fictional story incorporating all three, with a beginning, a complication, and a resolution. 3) Keep it playful - perfection is not the point. 4) Audience can call out a new element to weave in mid-story for an advanced version. 5) Rotate storytellers with fresh suggestions.
variations: Solo: roll random character/setting/problem from generators and record a 2-minute tale

name: Apples to Apples Debate
description: Pairs draw a random word (from cards or a list) and must build a debatable topic from it, then run a compressed two-sided debate. Trains topic generation plus argument under time.
instructions: 1) Use Apples-to-Apples cards or any random-word list. 2) Each pair draws a word and invents a debatable resolution connected to it ('Apples are overrated', 'Cities should ban cars'). 3) Run the round: 5 minutes prep, 2-minute opening each side, 1 minute of questions each, 1-minute closing each. 4) A judge or the room votes and names the most persuasive moment. 5) Swap words and sides.
variations: Faster micro-version: 1 minute prep, 30-second speeches each side

name: Morality on the Spot (Role Discussion)
description: Groups of four take fixed discussion roles (Presenter, Clarifier, Elaborator, Devil's Advocate) to talk through a moral dilemma. Trains specific contribution styles for group discussion and debate.
instructions: 1) Form groups of four; assign roles: PRESENTER (introduces the issue and an initial opinion), CLARIFIER (asks for definitions and details), ELABORATOR (builds on others' points without taking a side), DEVIL'S ADVOCATE (raises opposing views and 'what if' scenarios). 2) Draw a moral question card ('Is it ever right to lie?'). 3) Discuss for 5-10 minutes, each person playing only their role. 4) Rotate roles with a new question so everyone practices each contribution style. 5) Debrief which role was hardest and why.
variations: Add a Synthesizer role who must summarize all positions at the end

name: Wordsmith (Sharpen the Claim)
description: One person states an argumentative claim; each successive person restates it with fewer words or more powerful word choices. Trains concision and word-level persuasive punch.
instructions: 1) First person states a full-sentence argumentative claim ('We should reduce screen time because it harms our attention spans'). 2) The next person restates the same claim using FEWER words while keeping the meaning. 3) The next person restates it again with MORE powerful, vivid word choices. 4) Continue around until the claim is as tight and punchy as the group can make it. 5) Compare the first and final versions aloud.
variations: Solo: write a thesis, then rewrite it three times - shorter, then stronger, then more vivid

name: Justify It
description: Person A makes any statement (believed or not); Person B must immediately explain why it's true. Trains rapid reason generation and supporting a position you didn't choose.
instructions: 1) Person A states something - 'Mondays are the best day of the week', 'pineapple belongs on pizza'. 2) Person B must immediately justify WHY it is true, giving at least one solid reason, with no hedging. 3) Swap roles with a new statement. 4) Raise difficulty by requiring 2 then 3 distinct reasons each time, delivered without pausing. 5) Keep statements increasingly absurd to stretch invention.
variations: On the Flip Side variant: after justifying, the same person must immediately argue the opposite

name: On the Flip Side
description: After any statement is made, the responder says 'On the flip side...' and delivers the opposing argument on the spot. Isolates and drills quick counterargument generation.
instructions: 1) Person A states a position. 2) Person B responds 'On the flip side...' and immediately argues the opposite case with at least one reason. 3) Person A can then flip it again, and so on, ping-ponging viewpoints. 4) No pausing allowed between 'flip side' and the argument. 5) Swap who starts and use new topics. The aim is reflexive ability to see and voice the other side.
variations: Solo: state an opinion aloud, then immediately argue against yourself

name: Take Action (Problem-to-Plan)
description: Draw a card naming a societal or everyday problem and, in one minute, propose a course of action and justify why it solves the problem. Trains solution-oriented persuasive speaking under time.
instructions: 1) Write 10 problems on index cards (mundane to societal: 'the office coffee is always cold', 'local park is littered', 'team meetings run long'). 2) Draw one and start a 1-minute timer. 3) Speak: name the problem, propose a specific course of action, and justify why it would actually solve it. 4) Draw the next card. 5) Group or solo with audio recording. The discipline is concrete action plus reasoning, not just complaint.
variations: Add a required call to action aimed at a specific decision-maker

name: Blow Up the Balloon (Consequence Chain)
description: Build a chain of consequences around a circle, each person adding 'which leads to...' with a bigger impact, escalating to absurdity. Trains impact analysis and the consequence-reasoning used in debate.
instructions: 1) Sit in a circle; first person makes a small statement ('I skipped breakfast'). 2) Next person adds 'which leads to...' with a logical next consequence ('...which leads to being hungry by 10am'). 3) Each person continues the chain, making the impacts progressively bigger. 4) Escalate until the consequences become absurdly enormous, 'popping the balloon'. 5) Debrief: the drill teaches mapping short- and long-term consequences - the backbone of impact arguments.
variations: Reverse causation: start from a huge event and trace backward 'which was caused by...'

name: Pulled From the Headlines (1-Minute News Summary)
description: Grab a random news article and summarize it aloud in one minute, no prep, making it intriguing, clear, and concise. Daily habit-stack for fluent, structured extemporaneous speaking.
instructions: 1) Open any news app and pick a random article. 2) Read it once. 3) With no further prep, deliver a 1-minute spoken summary that is intriguing (hook the listener), clear (one main point), and concise (no rambling). 4) Record it or deliver to a partner. 5) Do this daily; over time it builds the current-events fluency that powers impromptu and extemp speaking.
variations: Pair version: summarize to a partner who then asks one follow-up you must answer

name: Hot Seat Q&A
description: One person sits while the group fires questions at them for 1-3 minutes, answering each on the spot. Trains composure, quick answers, and Q&A poise in a supportive setting.
instructions: 1) One person takes the 'hot seat'; the rest form the questioners. 2) Set norms: the person may 'pass', questions must be meaningful (not gotcha), no repeats. 3) For 1-3 minutes, the group fires questions and the person answers each immediately and concisely. 4) Advanced storyteller version: the person must spin a quick story inspired by three words the group shouts. 5) Rotate so everyone sits.
variations: In-character hot seat: answer as a famous person or as your future self

name: Talking Code (Flowing Practice)
description: A speaker delivers 2-3 arguments while listeners capture them in abbreviations, symbols, and shorthand. Trains the active-listening and note-taking ('flowing') skill that powers rebuttal and Q&A.
instructions: 1) One person delivers 2-3 arguments on a simple prompt at a steady pace. 2) Listeners take notes using as few full words as possible - abbreviations, arrows, symbols, codes - capturing the structure and key claims. 3) After, a listener reconstructs the speech aloud from their shorthand. 4) Compare reconstructions: who caught the most with the least writing? 5) Speed up delivery as listeners improve.
origin: The Practice Space public-speaking warm-ups; competitive debate 'flowing'
variations: Flow-and-rebut: after flowing, immediately deliver a rebuttal off your notes

name: Extend O'Rama
description: Two debaters pick one claim and trade alternating one-minute speeches, each extending and answering the other's evidence. Trains depth on a single argument rather than spreading thin.
instructions: 1) Two people choose one debate claim (e.g., 'economic decline causes war'). 2) Person A presents an initial piece of evidence/reasoning supporting their side. 3) Person B responds with a direct counter, using the '3 Rs and C' habit: Reference (what they said), Refute, Reason, Compare. 4) Alternate 1-minute speeches, each side deepening and answering on this one claim. 5) Continue for several rounds; the focus is extending and clashing on a single point, not introducing new arguments.
variations: Card-war version using real evidence cards on each side

name: Card Flowing Drill
description: One person reads off random playing cards while listeners 'flow' (note) them as if they were arguments, with the reader switching between imaginary speeches. A pure note-taking and organization drill.
instructions: 1) Two or more people; one holds a deck. 2) The reader draws and announces cards ('Queen of Hearts', 'Three of Clubs') at speaking pace. 3) Everyone else flows the cards onto paper as if they were arguments, keeping them organized in columns. 4) The reader randomly switches between different 'speeches' (e.g., 'now the negative block'), and listeners must move their flow to the right column. 5) Compare flows for completeness and organization.
variations: Use real short arguments instead of cards once organization is solid

name: Categories (Definition Debate Circle)
description: Players in a circle name items in an agreed category in turn; disputed answers trigger a mini-debate the group votes on. Trains quick recall, definitions, and on-the-spot argument.
instructions: 1) Agree on a category (soda brands, breakfast cereals, types of dance). 2) Stand in a circle; going clockwise, each player must say a valid answer within a few seconds, no repeats. 3) Anyone who blanks, repeats, or times out is out. 4) If a player objects that an answer doesn't fit the category, both sides give a 15-second argument and the remaining players vote on validity. 5) Last player standing wins. The debate-over-borderline-cases is the real skill.
variations: Themed to a topic area you're studying to build domain vocabulary

name: Flow and Judge a Debate
description: Watch a recorded debate, take complete notes (flow), then write a reasoned decision actively seeking the losing side's best case first. Trains listening, weighing, and seeing all sides of an argument.
instructions: 1) Get a recorded debate (round footage or any structured debate video). 2) Flow the whole thing: track every argument and response in organized columns. 3) Before deciding, deliberately build the strongest case for the side you think LOST. 4) Then write a clear decision explaining who won and why, citing specific clash points. 5) Compare with the actual result or a friend's ballot. The discipline of arguing for the underdog first kills confirmation bias.
variations: Judge a panel show or a real political debate and write a ballot

name: Expert Presentation (Ridiculous Topic Authority)
description: Receive a random, ridiculous subject and deliver a confident 2-minute speech persuading the audience the issue is urgent. Trains projected authority and conviction independent of content.
instructions: 1) Someone gives you a random absurd subject ('the global shortage of left socks', 'why pigeons are spying on us'). 2) Immediately deliver a 2-minute speech as the world expert: raise awareness, cite invented studies, propose action, sound completely authoritative. 3) The rule is total commitment - confident posture, gestures, gravitas - while spouting baloney. 4) Audience rates conviction, not accuracy. 5) Debrief which delivery choices created the impression of expertise.
variations: Slide version overlaps with PowerPoint Karaoke; add hostile Q&A at the end

name: Foreign Film Dubbing
description: Two people act a scene in gibberish while two others provide the live English 'dub', matching lip movements and emotion. Trains vocal expressiveness, timing, and reading nonverbal cues.
instructions: 1) Ask the audience for the title of a foreign film that never existed. 2) Two players perform a scene from it speaking only gibberish, with full emotion and gesture. 3) Two offstage 'dubbers' watch the actors' mouths and supply English dialogue in sync with the lip movements, matching tone and emotion. 4) Swap roles so everyone practices both acting and dubbing. 5) The dubbers' skill is matching vocal emotion and timing to body language - the core of expressive delivery.
variations: Simple Gibberish Translation: one person speaks gibberish, a partner translates into a coherent speech

name: Acceptance Speech Game
description: A host announces a made-up award and points to you; you must instantly deliver an emotional acceptance speech for it. Trains spontaneous sentiment, structure, and warmth on demand.
instructions: 1) A host invents an absurd award ('Best Use of a Stapler', 'Most Improved at Parallel Parking') and points to a player. 2) That player walks up and delivers a 30-60 second acceptance speech: surprise, thanks to specific (invented) people, a heartfelt story, a closing line. 3) Commit emotionally - tears optional, sincerity required. 4) The host invents a new award and points to the next person. 5) Debrief: who built a real arc (humility, gratitude, message) in under a minute?
