origin: improv performance game (Improv Notes; New York Improv Theater)
variations: Toast version: deliver an impromptu wedding/retirement toast for a random named person

name: Yes-And Build for Speakers
description: In pairs, each line must begin 'Yes, and...' building on the partner's last statement to plan something together. Trains listening, acceptance, and fluid building - the basis of confident on-the-fly speaking and Q&A.
instructions: 1) Pair up and pick a shared goal to plan ('let's plan a party', 'let's design a city'). 2) Person A offers an idea. 3) Person B must respond starting with 'Yes, and...' accepting it and adding to it. 4) Alternate, every line beginning 'Yes, and...', never blocking or negating. 5) Run 2-3 minutes, then debrief how it felt to be accepted vs. how tempting it was to say 'yes, but'. Use the same accept-and-build reflex when fielding tough questions live.
origin: Viola Spolin / improv tradition, adapted for speakers
variations: Yes-and your own ideas solo: brainstorm a topic by accepting and extending each thought aloud

name: Gibberish Speech (Jabberwocky Drill)
description: Deliver a 'speech' in pure gibberish or nonsense text (like Lewis Carroll's Jabberwocky), conveying meaning entirely through tone, rhythm, gesture, and expression. Isolates delivery from content.
instructions: 1) Write a few lines of made-up gibberish words, or use 'Jabberwocky' as your script. 2) Deliver it as if it's a real, important speech - a rallying call, a sales pitch, a eulogy - using full vocal variety, gestures, pauses, eye contact, and emotion. 3) Have listeners guess the 'genre' and mood; if they can read your intent without real words, your delivery is doing its job. 4) Re-deliver the same gibberish in a contrasting emotion. 5) Then deliver a real passage and notice your delivery carrying more.
variations: Gibberish debate: two people argue in gibberish with full conviction; audience judges who 'won' on delivery alone

name: Speaker's Vocal Warm-Up Stack
description: A short stacked routine of humming, lip/tongue trills, pitch sirens, and yawn-sighs that warms the voice, opens resonance, and steadies the breath before speaking.
instructions: 1) HUM gently with lips closed for 30 seconds, feeling the buzz in your face/lips; this warms the cords without strain. 2) LIP TRILLS: blow air through loosely closed lips to make a 'brrr', gliding up and down in pitch (add tongue trills 'rrrr' too). 3) SIRENS: on 'oooo' or 'ng', slide smoothly from your lowest comfortable pitch to your highest and back, several times, to expand range and smooth breaks. 4) YAWN-SIGH: trigger a yawn to lift the soft palate, then sigh out on voice from high to low to release tension. 5) Finish with a few resonant 'maa-may-mee-moh-moo' slides. Do the full stack before any talk.
origin: voice/voiceover pedagogy (Science of People, Teleprompter, 30 Day Singer)
variations: Straw phonation: hum/glide through a drinking straw into water for gentle cord warmup

name: Story Spine Speech
description: Tell a story aloud by filling in the Pixar 'story spine' template, which guarantees a complete arc with setup, turning point, escalation, and resolution. Trains reliable narrative structure for speeches.
instructions: 1) Learn the spine: 'Once upon a time ___. Every day ___. One day ___. Because of that ___. (repeat 'because of that' 1-3 times). Until finally ___. And ever since then ___.' 2) Pick a topic (a real event, a business case, a made-up tale) and fill each slot aloud as you tell it. 3) Deliver the whole story in 2-3 minutes, hitting every beat. 4) Note how the 'one day' is your inciting incident and 'until finally' is your climax. 5) Re-tell a different story on the same spine until the structure is automatic.
origin: Kenn Adams' Story Spine, popularized by Pixar (Emma Coats)
variations: Apply the spine to a persuasive talk: frame your argument as a story with this skeleton

name: Point of Information Drill
description: Practice both offering crisp 15-second points of information during a speaker's speech and answering them smoothly without losing your thread. Trains composure under interruption and concise challenge.
instructions: 1) One person delivers a 3-4 minute speech on a motion. 2) Others stand to offer POIs (only after the first minute, before the last minute); a POI is a 15-second pointed question or rebuttal. 3) The speaker chooses when to accept (taking 1-2 per minute), answers concisely, and returns to their argument without losing momentum. 4) Offerers practice making POIs sharp and respectful - no badgering. 5) Rotate so everyone practices both delivering under interruption and crafting tight challenges.
variations: Heckle-resilience version: friendly hecklers interject and the speaker must absorb and continue

name: Moderated Caucus Opening (30-90s Position Speech)
description: Deliver a tightly timed 30-90 second speech that opens with a hook, states a clear position, and proposes one actionable solution. The Model UN drill for punchy, structured short speeches.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic and a 'position' (a country, a stakeholder, or just your own view) and a speaking time of 30, 60, or 90 seconds. 2) Jot bullet points, not a script. 3) Deliver: a HOOK to grab attention (statistic, image, question), a clear STATEMENT of your position, and one ACTIONABLE solution or proposal. 4) Hit the time limit exactly. 5) Repeat with new topics and shorter times. The constraint forces every second to earn its place.
origin: Model United Nations training (Best Delegate, MUNUC)
variations: Defend Your Favorite: argue why your favorite film/album is the best in exactly 30 seconds to learn to fill time

name: Political Gaffe Spin Drill
description: Given a scandal or awkward scenario, you have 45 seconds to formulate and deliver a defense, explanation, or spin. Trains poise and persuasive reframing under pressure.
instructions: 1) A partner presents a sticky scenario: 'A leaked email shows you criticized your own team', 'you were caught on camera asleep in a meeting'. 2) Take a beat, then deliver a 45-second response that defends, explains, or spins the situation persuasively and calmly. 3) The listener judges whether you'd have changed their opinion. 4) Draw a new scenario and repeat. 5) Advanced: the listener fires one hostile follow-up you must field.
variations: Bridge it: practice the 'I understand the concern, but the real issue is...' pivot for hostile Q&A

name: Fishbowl Discussion
description: A small inner circle discusses or debates a topic while an outer circle silently observes and then gives feedback. Trains speaking under observation and sharpens the observers' analytical ear.
instructions: 1) Form an inner circle of 4-6 speakers and an outer circle of observers. 2) The inner circle discusses or debates a topic aloud for 5-10 minutes; only they may speak. 3) Observers watch assigned dimensions: clarity, evidence, body language, listening, who dominates. 4) Swap circles and repeat with a new topic. 5) Observers deliver targeted feedback to specific speakers. An empty 'hot seat' chair in the inner circle lets an observer tap in temporarily.
origin: discussion pedagogy; used in Model UN and classrooms (Best Delegate)
variations: Debate fishbowl with assigned sides; tap-in chair for fresh voices

name: Rapid-Fire Objection Handling
description: A partner machine-guns common objections at you and you must calmly answer each using a Feature-Benefit-Evidence response. Trains persuasive composure and structured rebuttal of pushback.
instructions: 1) List the common objections to your pitch/idea (too expensive, no time, why you, competitors do it cheaper, not now). 2) A partner fires them at you rapidly, one after another. 3) For each, respond calmly with Feature-Benefit-Evidence: acknowledge, state the relevant feature, translate to a benefit for THEM, and back it with a proof point or example. 4) Don't get defensive; treat each objection as a question. 5) Loop the toughest objections until your answers are smooth and confident.
variations: Solo: write your 10 hardest objections and record yourself answering each cold in under 30 seconds

name: Reframe Anxiety as Excitement
description: Just before speaking, say aloud 'I am excited' and relabel your nervous arousal as excitement rather than fighting it. A research-backed quick reframe that improves performance under pressure.
instructions: 1) Notice pre-speech symptoms (racing heart, jitters) - these are high-arousal, the same physiology as excitement. 2) Instead of trying to 'calm down', say out loud (or firmly to yourself) 'I am excited' several times. 3) Channel the energy: tell yourself this talk is an opportunity, picture the upside. 4) Walk on with that excited framing. 5) Practice it before every low-stakes speaking rep so it's automatic when stakes are high. (Brooks 2014 found this reframe improved performance ~17%.)
origin: Alison Wood Brooks, Harvard (2014) 'Get Excited' research
variations: Pair with a 2-minute confident posture hold before walking on

name: Success Visualization Rehearsal
description: Vividly rehearse the entire speaking experience in your mind - the room, your calm confident delivery, the audience's positive response - to build familiarity and cut anxiety. Mental reps fire the same neural pathways as physical practice.
instructions: 1) Sit quietly, eyes closed, breathing slowly. 2) Mentally walk through the whole event in first person: arriving, the room and audience, walking up calmly, delivering your opening line clearly, moving through your points with poise, handling a question well, finishing strong to warm applause. 3) Engage senses - see faces, hear your steady voice, feel the clicker. 4) Replay any wobble going RIGHT this time. 5) Do a full visualization the night before and a brief one minutes before going on.
origin: sports psychology applied to public speaking; write-out-loud and coaching write-ups
variations: Worst-case rehearsal: visualize something going wrong and yourself recovering gracefully, to defang the fear

name: Slash-Mark Pausing Drill
description: Mark a passage with single and double slashes for short and long pauses, then read it aloud honoring every mark. Trains deliberate phrasing, the power pause, and emphasis.
instructions: 1) Print a passage of your speech. 2) Mark it: single slash (/) for a short within-sentence pause, double slash (//) for a longer full stop, and underline the 1-2 words per sentence you'll stress. 3) Read it aloud honoring every mark exactly, holding the double-slash pauses a full beat or two. 4) Pay special attention to pausing right before AND after your most important line, letting it land. 5) Record and check that the pauses sound intentional and powerful, not hesitant.
origin: oral-reading fluency pedagogy and speech coaching (write-out-loud)
variations: Silence-counting version: insert a deliberate 'one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand' pause after each key sentence

name: Eulogy Rehearsal Protocol
description: A structured rehearsal for an emotional occasion speech (eulogy/tribute): repeated read-throughs that desensitize the emotional spots and lock in slow, clear delivery. Trains composure when speaking about something that moves you.
instructions: 1) Write the eulogy word-for-word, 3-5 minutes long, built on one specific story that shows the person's character. 2) Read it aloud many times - rehearsing repeatedly softens the emotional charge so you can get through it live. 3) Mark the spots where you choke up; plan a slow breath and a pause there rather than pushing through. 4) Practice in front of one trusted person for feedback on pace and warmth. 5) Final runs: speak deliberately slowly, enunciate, and make eye contact every few sentences. Use 4-7-8 breathing right before.
setup: a written eulogy or tribute (real or practice)
variations: Practice on a fictional honoree to build the skill before you ever need it

name: Commonplace Amplification (Progymnasmata VII)
description: Deliver a speech that amplifies and attacks a recognized type of wrongdoer or vice (the tyrant, the traitor, the miser) rather than a specific person. The classical drill for emotional, indignant persuasion.
instructions: 1) Pick a type, not a person: 'the corrupt politician', 'the bully', 'the cheat'. 2) Build the speech on the classical heads: a contrary (briefly note the opposite virtue), exposition of the deeds of this type, comparison (this type is worse than X), a turn to the audience's emotions (indignation, fear), and the demand for judgment. 3) Deliver 3-4 minutes with rising intensity. 4) Because the audience already agrees the vice is bad, your job is pure amplification - making them FEEL it. 5) Note which intensifiers and rhythms raised the heat.
variations: Flip to amplify a virtue/type of hero ('the whistleblower') for inspirational speaking

name: Synkrisis (Comparison Speech)
description: Deliver a structured speech comparing two people, things, or ideas point by point and concluding which is superior. The classical drill for balanced, comparative argument and weighing.
instructions: 1) Choose two comparable subjects (two leaders, city vs. country, books vs. films). 2) Compare them through parallel heads in the same order for each: origin, qualities, deeds/effects, value. 3) For each head, weigh them against each other rather than describing separately ('whereas A offers..., B by contrast...'). 4) Conclude by declaring which is superior and why, acknowledging the loser's merits. 5) Deliver in 3-5 minutes. The skill is true comparison, not two back-to-back descriptions.
variations: Debate-flavored: compare two policy options and recommend one to a decision-maker

name: Introduction of a Law (Progymnasmata XIV)
description: Compose and deliver a speech proposing a new law or attacking a proposed one, arguing from legality, justice, expediency, and practicality. The capstone deliberative exercise of classical rhetoric.
instructions: 1) Draft or pick a proposed law ('ban phones in schools', 'mandatory voting'). 2) Argue FOR it (or against) through the standard heads: is it LEGAL/constitutional, JUST, EXPEDIENT (does it produce good outcomes), POSSIBLE/practical to enforce, and HONORABLE. 3) Raise and answer the strongest objection within the speech. 4) Deliver 3-5 minutes as if to a legislature. 5) Then flip and argue the opposite side using the mirrored heads. The two-sided practice builds deliberative range.
variations: Mini-version: a 60-second 'I move that...' speech for a club or meeting motion

name: Maxim Expansion (Progymnasmata IV)
description: Take an anonymous maxim or proverb and expand it into a short speech using the chreia heads. Like the chreia drill but with an unattributed saying, training development of a single idea.
instructions: 1) Pick a proverb or maxim ('A stitch in time saves nine', 'Knowledge is power'). 2) Expand it through the heads: paraphrase it in your own words; give the reason it's true; state the contrary (what happens if ignored); offer an analogy; give an example from life/history; cite a supporting authority; close urging the listener to live by it. 3) Deliver 2-4 minutes. 4) Practice until you can run the structure on any proverb impromptu. 5) The difference from chreia: no named author to praise, so you lead with paraphrase.
variations: Disagree version: argue why a popular proverb is actually wrong

name: Cross-Examination Drill
description: Practice asking a tight sequence of short, leading questions to extract concessions from a partner defending a claim, then locking those concessions in. Trains controlled questioning and Q&A dominance.
instructions: 1) Your partner defends the main claim of a short news editorial. 2) You cross-examine for 2 minutes using only short, one-idea questions, ideally answerable yes/no, aimed at exposing gaps or extracting admissions. 3) When they concede something useful, LOCK IT DOWN: restate it, get them to confirm, and note it. 4) Don't argue - just ask and pin. 5) Swap roles. Advanced: partner gives evasive, long-winded answers and you must redirect them back. Afterward, list every concession you won.
variations: Witness version: you defend and a partner cross-examines you, training calm, brief answers under pressure

name: Five Ways to Open
description: Write and deliver five different openings for the SAME talk - a startling stat, a rhetorical question, a personal story, a bold statement, and a vivid scene - then pick the strongest. Isolates and trains the hook.
instructions: 1) Take one talk topic. 2) Craft five distinct 20-30 second openings: (a) a surprising statistic or fact, (b) a rhetorical question (with a deliberate pause after), (c) a short personal story/anecdote, (d) a bold or provocative statement, (e) a vivid scene that drops the listener into a moment. 3) Deliver all five aloud back to back. 4) Have a listener (or your recorder) judge which hooked hardest and why. 5) Rehearse the winner more than any other line in your talk.
origin: speech-opening pedagogy (Project Charisma, Teleprompter, American Express)
variations: Do the same for closings: write five different final lines (call to action, callback, quote, challenge, vision)

name: Rhetorical Question Loop
description: Open a talk with a rhetorical question, hold a real pause, and deliberately answer it minutes later to close the loop. Trains audience engagement and structural payoff.
instructions: 1) Craft a rhetorical question that frames your whole talk ('What would you do with one more hour each day?'). 2) Deliver it, then PAUSE a full 2-3 seconds so listeners actually think - resist rushing to the answer. 3) Proceed with your content. 4) Near the end, explicitly return and answer the opening question, closing the loop for a satisfying finish. 5) Practice the pause length on recording - most speakers rush it. Drill several different framing questions for one topic.
variations: Call-and-response version: ask a question expecting a show of hands or a shouted answer, and practice handling whatever the room does

name: Evaluation Sandwich Practice
description: Watch a speaker (live or recorded) and deliver a structured 2-3 minute spoken evaluation using the commend-recommend-commend sandwich. Trains the analytical ear and the skill of public, constructive feedback.
instructions: 1) Watch a speech, taking notes against set criteria: vocal variety, eye contact, gestures, structure, clarity. 2) Prepare a 2-3 minute spoken evaluation in three layers: COMMEND (specific things done well, with examples), RECOMMEND (one or two concrete improvements, phrased as suggestions), COMMEND (an encouraging close). 3) Deliver it aloud as if to the speaker and a group. 4) Keep it specific and kind, never vague ('good job') or harsh. 5) Doing this regularly sharpens your eye for the exact habits to fix in your own speaking.
setup: a speech to watch; evaluation criteria
origin: Toastmasters evaluation method (Pathways Evaluation and Feedback project)
variations: Self-evaluation: record your own talk and deliver the sandwich evaluation aloud about yourself

name: Think-Pair-Share Facilitation
description: Practice running a Think-Pair-Share: pose a question, give silent think-time, have the audience discuss in pairs, then field shares - and manage the room throughout. Trains interactive facilitation and handling audience response.
instructions: 1) Prepare a discussion question tied to your talk. 2) In front of a practice group, pose it and give 30 seconds of SILENT think time (resist filling the silence). 3) Direct people to turn to a neighbor and discuss for 1-2 minutes; circulate. 4) Call the room back and field 2-3 shares, paraphrasing and bridging each into your next point. 5) Debrief on your transitions and timekeeping. The hard skills are giving real silence, regaining attention, and weaving audience answers into your message.
variations: Polling version: practice posing a nonverbal poll ('hands up if...') and reacting live to the result

name: Five-Second Moment Story Drill
description: Boil a personal story down to the single five-second moment when something changed inside you, and build the telling around that beat. Matthew Dicks' core method for stories that actually land.
instructions: 1) Recall an experience you want to tell. 2) Hunt for the five-second moment of internal CHANGE - the instant you realized, decided, forgave, broke, understood. If you can't find one, it's not yet a story. 3) Make that moment your ending; everything before it exists to set it up by contrast (show how you were BEFORE). 4) Cut anything that doesn't drive toward that beat. 5) Tell it in 3-5 minutes, landing on the moment of change. 6) Practice it until you can tell it from memory, timed under the limit.
origin: Matthew Dicks, 'Storyworthy'; The Moth storytelling tradition
variations: Homework for Life: each night, note the most story-worthy moment of your day to build a moment bank

name: Count to 20 (Group Listening)
description: A group tries to count to twenty aloud with random people calling out each number; if two speak at once, restart at one. A listening-and-timing warmup that builds the group attunement underlying natural turn-taking.
instructions: 1) Stand or sit in a circle, eyes open (or closed for harder). 2) Anyone can say 'one'; then anyone says 'two', and so on, with no set order and no signaling who goes next. 3) If two people speak at the same time, the whole group restarts at 'one'. 4) Reach twenty by tuning into each other's breath, micro-pauses, and energy. 5) Debrief: what nonverbal cues let you sense when to speak vs. wait? That sensitivity transfers to reading rooms and panels.
origin: improv warmup (Spolin tradition; widely used in speaker training)
variations: Sound ball / pass-the-clap rhythm games for the same attunement

name: Conduct the Speaker (Dynamics Dial)
description: A partner 'conducts' you like an orchestra - raising and lowering a hand for volume, speeding or slowing for pace - while you deliver, instantly matching your dynamics to their cues. Builds conscious control of vocal range.
instructions: 1) Begin delivering a passage or impromptu speech. 2) Your partner conducts: hand high = louder, low = softer; fast circles = speed up, slow = slow down; fist = intensity up, open palm = ease off. 3) You continuously match your voice to their gestures without stopping the speech. 4) They deliberately push you to extremes you'd never naturally hit. 5) Swap roles. 6) Then deliver once unconducted and notice your expanded range. Numbers variant: they hold up 1-10 fingers and you scale volume/energy to that number.
origin: drama/vocal coaching; Practice Space dynamics variants
variations: Self-conduct: pre-mark your script with volume/pace symbols and deliver to your own plan

name: Alphabet Over-Enunciation
description: Recite the alphabet slowly with hugely exaggerated mouth movement, drawing out every sound. A fast articulation and face-warmup before speaking.
instructions: 1) Stand and open your mouth and eyes wide. 2) Slowly say the alphabet, A to Z, drawing out and over-shaping every single letter sound with exaggerated lips, jaw, and tongue. 3) Really 'chew' each sound; feel the face muscles working. 4) Do it once slow and big, then once at speaking pace keeping the crispness. 5) Group version: do it in unison as a warmup. Use right before a talk to wake up your articulators.
variations: Say the alphabet as if it's a love poem, an argument, a sales pitch - emotion over the letters

name: Count the Sounds (Pre-Speech Focus)
description: Close your eyes and count every distinct sound you can hear, then turn them into a rhythm. A quick grounding and focus reset that pulls you into the present before speaking.
instructions: 1) Close your eyes and breathe slowly. 2) Listen deeply to your environment and silently count every distinct sound you can pick out - a hum, distant traffic, your own breath. 3) Try to find one or two more than seemed possible. 4) Optionally turn the sounds into a simple rhythm or pattern in your head. 5) Open your eyes feeling present and externally focused rather than spiraling in pre-speech nerves. Use right before walking on.
variations: Grounding 5-4-3-2-1 version (5 things you see, 4 you hear, etc.) before going on

name: Balderdash (Invented Definition)
description: Given an obscure or nonsense word, invent and confidently deliver a plausible definition (and origin) on the spot. Trains confident bluffing, invention, and authoritative delivery.
instructions: 1) A neighbor gives you an obscure real word (or a made-up one). 2) Without hesitation, deliver a plausible-sounding definition aloud - and for extra challenge, invent its part of speech, country of origin, etymology, and a sentence using it. 3) Others vote on whether they'd believe it. 4) In the full game, mix your fake definition with the real one and others guess which is true. 5) The skill is committing to invented detail with total authority - the same muscle as fielding a question you don't know the answer to.
origin: the party game Balderdash / Call My Bluff, adapted for speaking practice
variations: Etymology theater: present the fake word as a TED-style mini-lecture for 60 seconds

name: Two Truths and a Lie (Spoken)
description: State two true things and one lie about yourself, delivering all three so convincingly the audience can't tell which is false. Trains congruent, believable delivery and reading an audience.
instructions: 1) Prepare two true statements and one false one about yourself. 2) Deliver all three aloud with identical confidence, eye contact, and detail - the goal is to make the lie sound exactly as true as the truths. 3) Audience questions you about each; answer in character without leaking tells. 4) They vote on the lie. 5) Reveal. Debrief: which delivery tells (hesitation, less detail, broken eye contact) gave away the lie? Those are the same tells that undermine you when you speak truthfully but nervously.
origin: classic icebreaker adapted for delivery practice
variations: Three stories, one false: tell three short anecdotes, one invented, and have listeners spot the fake

name: Would You Rather Defense
description: Pick between two (often silly) options and immediately deliver a persuasive case for your choice. A fast, low-stakes drill for taking a position and defending it on demand.
instructions: 1) Someone poses a 'would you rather' ('...have the ability to fly or be invisible?', '...always be 10 minutes late or 20 minutes early?'). 2) Instantly pick a side - no fence-sitting. 3) Deliver a 30-60 second persuasive case: a clear reason, a vivid example or scenario, and a confident conclusion. 4) Optionally a partner argues the other side and the room votes. 5) Rapid-fire several in a row. The point is decisiveness plus instant justification.
origin: classic conversation game adapted for impromptu speaking
variations: Assigned-side version: you must defend the option you'd personally reject

name: Keyword Reduction Rehearsal
description: Rehearse a talk by progressively stripping a full script down to a detailed outline and then to a bare keyword list, delivering each round from less text. Builds memorization that sounds natural, not recited.
instructions: 1) Write the talk word-for-word and read it aloud once. 2) Reduce it to a detailed outline (full points, no full sentences) and deliver from that, filling in wording live. 3) Reduce again to a keyword skeleton - one or two trigger words per section - and deliver, generating sentences fresh each time. 4) Finally deliver from memory with no notes. 5) Because each pass forces active recall and fresh phrasing, you internalize ideas, not a script, so you can't 'lose your place'. Spread passes over several days.
variations: Combine with Memory Palace: assign each keyword to a location in a familiar room

name: Memory Palace Speech
description: Memorize a talk's sequence by placing each section as a vivid image along a familiar mental route (rooms of your home), then 'walk' the route to recall it in order. The memory-champion method for never losing your place.
instructions: 1) Choose a familiar journey with distinct stops - rooms of your house, your commute. 2) Chunk your talk into its main sections (intro, point 1, point 2, story, call to action). 3) Place each section at a stop as a vivid, weird, exaggerated image that encodes its content (e.g., a giant clock for your 'time' point on the kitchen table). 4) Rehearse by mentally walking the route in order, letting each image trigger that section. 5) Deliver the talk by 'walking' the palace. Because the route is fixed, your section order is locked in.
origin: method of loci (ancient mnemonic; used by memory champions)
variations: Use the fingers of one hand as a five-stop mini-palace for a short speech

name: Grounded Stance (Oak Tree Drill)
description: Practice a stable, grounded speaking stance - feet planted shoulder-width, weight even, no swaying - imagining roots going deep into the floor. Builds the steady physical presence that reads as confidence.
instructions: 1) Stand with feet planted firmly, roughly armpit/shoulder width apart, weight evenly on both feet. 2) Imagine you're a 300-year-old oak with roots going deep and wide - firm, unshakeable. 3) Deliver the first 30 seconds of your talk WITHOUT moving your feet at all, killing the nervous sway/rock/shift. 4) Notice the urge to crossed-legs, hip-lean, or feet-together 'good child' stances and resist them. 5) Once stillness is owned, allow only deliberate, planted steps for emphasis. Check in a mirror or on video.
origin: theatre grounding technique; speaker coaching (Genard Method, SlideModel)
variations: Pairs with the Newspaper Floor anti-pacing drill; add a 2-minute expansive power-pose hold beforehand

name: Minute to Win It (Topic Pull)
description: Everyone writes topics on slips into a pile; you pull one, get one minute to plan, then give a one-minute speech. A simple, scalable impromptu drill with peer-sourced surprise topics.
instructions: 1) Each participant writes 2-3 topics on slips and adds them to a central pile. 2) A speaker draws one at random. 3) One minute to plan: pick an angle and a rough beginning-middle-end. 4) Deliver a one-minute speech on it. 5) Pass to the next person. Solo version: build your own slip pile (or use a generator), draw blind, 60-second plan, 60-second speech, recorded. The peer-written topics tend to be weirder and harder than canned lists.
variations: Zero-prep version: speak the instant you read the slip; or pull and must connect two random slips

name: Declamation (Famous Speech Interpretation)
description: Take a previously delivered, publicly available speech and perform it as your own interpretation - same words, your voice, pauses, and emotion. Trains pure delivery: expression, dynamics, and command of language without writing burden.
instructions: 1) Choose a great speech (MLK, a famous commencement address, a movie monologue) of 3-10 minutes; trim to time. 2) Study its structure and emotional beats. 3) Memorize it, then perform it making your OWN delivery choices - your pacing, emphasis, pauses, gestures, and emotion - to communicate the ideas with clarity and feeling, NOT impersonating the original speaker. 4) Record and refine the vocal variety and emotional honesty. 5) Perform for a listener who gives feedback on whether the ideas and feeling landed.
variations: Contrast study: perform the same passage two opposite ways (somber vs. rousing) to feel how delivery changes meaning

name: Burden Mapping
description: Before any debate or persuasive speech, write out exactly what each side must prove to win, then build only the arguments that meet your burden. Trains strategic focus and argument prioritization.
instructions: 1) Take a resolution or persuasive claim. 2) Write down the BURDENS: what must the proposition prove (X, Y, Z) for the claim to hold, and what must the opposition prove or merely refute to defeat it. 3) For your side, list only the arguments that actually discharge your burden - cut anything that doesn't. 4) For the other side, predict which burden they'll attack and pre-build a response. 5) Then deliver a tight speech that explicitly meets your burden. This kills rambling and off-point arguments.
variations: Apply to a work pitch: write what you must prove to get a yes, and build only to that

name: The Politician's Pivot (Bridging Drill)
description: In a Q&A, answer every question by smoothly bridging away from it to the point you want to make ('That's not the real question - the real question is...'). Trains message discipline and graceful redirection under questioning.
instructions: 1) Have classmates or a partner fire questions at you, including off-topic or hostile ones. 2) For each, practice the bridge: briefly acknowledge, then pivot - 'That's a fair point, but what really matters here is...' or 'The bigger question is...' - and steer to YOUR key message. 3) Stay composed and never get trapped defending the premise of a bad question. 4) Do a round where you must bridge every single answer back to one core message. 5) Debrief which bridges felt natural vs. evasive; aim for smooth, not slippery.
setup: a partner or group to ask questions
origin: ModernBrain speech & debate drills; media-training technique
variations: Honest version: practice when NOT to bridge - answering a fair question directly builds trust

name: Rephrasing for Resonance
description: Take a speech that feels emotionally flat and re-deliver it sentence by sentence, spontaneously rephrasing each to convey the same meaning more powerfully without reusing the original keywords. Trains vivid language and emotional punch.
instructions: 1) Take a memorized or drafted speech section that feels lifeless. 2) Go sentence by sentence, re-saying each one out loud in a fresh, more vivid way - same meaning, different and stronger words, no reusing the original key terms. 3) Notice which spontaneous rephrasings hit harder than your written version. 4) Capture the best ones back into your script. 5) Repeat across the whole talk. The constraint of banning your original words forces richer language.
variations: Writer's-block rewrite: redo the entire speech on the same topic banning all your original analysis, jokes, sources, and examples

name: Connect the Example (Associative Speaking)
description: Announce which story or example you'll use BEFORE you know the topic, then receive a random topic and must build a one-minute speech connecting your pre-chosen example to it. Trains associative thinking and on-the-fly framing.
instructions: 1) Out loud, commit to an example or story you'll discuss (e.g., 'the time my flight got cancelled'). 2) A partner then gives you a random, unrelated topic ('ambition', 'trust', 'technology'). 3) You must deliver a one-minute speech that connects your pre-chosen story to that topic - finding the metaphorical or literal link live. 4) The forced order (story first, topic second) trains the exact associative muscle that lets you fit any anecdote to any prompt. 5) Repeat with new examples and topics.
variations: Build an example notebook over time so you always have material to draw from

name: Tweak Your Tone (Section Emotion Switch)
aliases: now I'm going to speak honestly drill
description: Before each paragraph of your talk, interrupt yourself to name and then adopt a fitting emotion ('Now, I'll speak about this ANGRILY... HONESTLY... PLAYFULLY'). Trains deliberate vocal-emotional variety across a speech.
instructions: 1) Take a prepared speech. 2) Identify the dominant emotion of your introduction. 3) Before delivering each subsequent paragraph, interrupt yourself out loud: 'Now I'm going to speak about this HONESTLY' (or angrily, tenderly, urgently, playfully), choosing the emotion that fits that section's content. 4) Then deliver that paragraph fully in that emotional color. 5) Run the whole talk this way. 6) Final pass: drop the spoken labels but keep the deliberate emotional shifts, so your delivery has mapped variety instead of one flat tone.
variations: Overlaps with Contrasting Colors; here the emotions are mapped to real speech sections rather than abstract practice lines

name: Cheat Sheet Challenge
description: Deliver a 5-10 minute speech from a cheat sheet holding only one word or short phrase per 15 seconds of content, generating all wording live. Bridges the gap between reading notes and full memorization.
instructions: 1) Take a talk you know the content of. 2) Build a cheat sheet with just one trigger word or short phrase for every ~15 seconds of speech (so a 5-minute talk has ~20 triggers). 3) Deliver the whole talk using only that sheet, inventing the actual sentences on the fly from each trigger. 4) Focus on smooth delivery and familiarity with the ideas, not exact wording. 5) Over reps, trim triggers further. The goal is confident speaking that's anchored but never read.
variations: Drop to one trigger per 30 then 60 seconds as you internalize the talk
